title: The body: its parts
hookLine: like a bag of mixed grain opened and looked at: hair, nails, teeth, skin (MN 10)

cards: Think how much of a day goes into what the body looks like. The mirror in the morning. The photo retaken four times.
The comparison that slips in while scrolling. The body becomes one picture, judged good or bad. The Satipatthana Sutta does something different.
It opens the body up, piece by piece, with the calm of a farmer checking stored grain.

teach.h: FROM THE SOLES UP, THE HEAD DOWN.
teach.b: The practitioner reviews this very body, the sutta says, from the soles of the feet up and from the top of the head down, bounded by skin and, in the sutta's blunt word, full of many kinds of impurity.
Then the list: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and on inward, organs and fluids, thirty-one parts in the sutta's list.
Later tradition added the brain to make thirty-two. Then the image.

teach.h: A BAG OF MIXED GRAIN, OPENED.
teach.b: A bag with an opening at both ends, full of mixed grain: hill rice, red rice, beans, peas, sesame, husked rice. A person with good eyes opens it and looks: this is rice, these are beans, this is sesame. Notice the tone.
They aren't disgusted, and they aren't admiring.
They're just sorting, clearly. That's the heart of the practice. In the Buddhist tradition, this contemplation is used to loosen two strong pulls: vanity about the body and craving for other bodies.
Some teachers stress the unattractiveness of the parts; others, especially today, stress simple, neutral seeing. Either way, the point is not to hate the body.
It's to see it as it is: not a single image to be judged, but a working collection of many things, each doing its job.
Hair is hair. Teeth are teeth. The picture in the mirror loosens its grip a little.

how: In Theravada monasteries, the first five parts (hair of the head, body hair, nails, teeth, skin) are traditionally taught to new monks and nuns at ordination; the contemplation of the thirty-two parts is recited and practiced to loosen vanity and craving.

o: something shameful to hate and keep hidden
many parts, sorted calmly, each just what it is
a single picture to be judged good or bad

games.q: match each piece of the simile.
p: hill rice, red rice, beans, sesame
the count once the brain is added

s: the practice is meant to make you hate your body
it's for seeing clearly and loosening vanity and craving, not for self-hatred.
the sutta's list has thirty-one parts; later tradition added the brain
the familiar count of thirty-two comes from the later list.
the grain simile is about sorting calmly
the person just sees: this is rice, these are beans.

games.q: you open a bag of mixed grain. what does the person in the sutta do?
o: look and sort: this is rice, these are beans.
admire how beautiful the grain is.
games.why: the person with good eyes simply sees each thing for what it is. the body is looked at the same way.

practice: Name ten parts of your body slowly, feeling each one if you can: hair, nails, teeth, skin, bones, muscles, heart, lungs, blood, breath. No admiring or wincing, just the calm of someone sorting grain: this is that.
If any part is painful or hard to think about today, skip it gently and move on.

wordCard.voice: The body, its parts. Opened like a bag of mixed grain and sorted calmly: hair, nails, teeth, skin, each one just what it is.

carryVoice: Your line: a bag of grain. Sorted, not judged: each part just what it is. Day two hundred fifty-three.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the parts of the body
